<reason>Both sides argued competently and stayed grounded in ordinary background knowledge. PRO built a coherent case on the severity/physics mechanism plus the structural externalities of stops (fatal encounters, racial disparity), and answered the pressure questions directly with the "speed lowers lethality of every crash type" pivot and the designate-the-driver fix. But CON kept the motion's conjunction live and landed the sharpest unanswered blow: cameras lower the speed of compliant, sign-reading drivers, not the impaired or distracted outliers who actually fill the morgue, so PRO's severity mechanism reaches the population least likely to die. PRO's closing restated the physics point but never addressed "whose speed" cameras lower. CON also answered PRO's marginal-yield question with a plausible targeting mechanism and the seatbelt example, and turned PRO's owner-liability fix back into "pay or inform on someone." PRO won the externalities prong more cleanly (CON's reform list does read as a concession), but CON's argument that PRO abandoned the "larger gains" prong went essentially uncontested at the end, making CON's route to victory the clearer one.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B4.4–B4.6 response to PRO's severity pivot: "whose speed does a camera lower?"—arguing cameras deter the sober, attentive driver while the drunk and the texting teen don't calculate envelope risk, so "PRO's mechanism works best on the drivers least likely to die." PRO's closing did not engage it.</best_rebuttal>
